scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Your question is more about **values, boundaries, and the nature of friendship vs. loyalty** than a simple moral judgment. Here’s a breakdown of the key ethical and emotional considerations, followed by my *personal* perspective (not a definitive answer, but a framework to reflect on): --- ### **Key Ethical Dilemmas in Your Situation** 1. **Loyalty to Friendship vs. Loyalty to Family** - You’re prioritizing a **13-year friendship** over your sister’s trust and feelings. That’s a huge ask, especially when the betrayal was directed at her. Many would argue this is unfair to her, as she’s the one who suffered the direct harm. - *Counterpoint*: You’re not *choosing* G over her—you’re choosing to **preserve a friendship that predates her relationship with G**, and you’re doing so with awareness (you know the throwaway account exists). But that doesn’t erase the emotional weight of her pain. 2. **Forgiveness vs. Accountability** - G’s remorse seems genuine, and you’ve forgiven him. That’s a personal choice, but forgiveness doesn’t always mean **ignoring the consequences** of his actions. Your sister may never feel safe around him again, even if you do. - *Question*: Is your forgiveness conditional? Do you expect G to prove himself over time, or are you holding him to a different standard than you would for a friend who betrayed *you*? 3. **The "Different Places" Excuse** - You’re right that physical distance might reduce friction in the future. But **emotional distance** doesn’t disappear just because you’re in different states. If G’s behavior is a recurring pattern, your sister’s pain won’t vanish with time. - *Counterpoint*: If you’re both mature adults in college, you *could* set clear boundaries (e.g., "We’re friends, but we don’t talk about her"). But that’s a lot to ask of a friendship built on decades of closeness. 4. **Your Sister’s Perspective** - She’s not just upset about the cheating—she’s upset that **you didn’t prioritize her feelings** over G’s. That’s a wound in itself. Even if you’re not "choosing sides," your actions (or inaction) send a message: *"Her pain isn’t as important as my friendship."* - *Ask yourself*: Would you want your best friend to stay close to someone who betrayed *you*? If not, why is this different? 5. **The Throwaway Account** - You mention both you and G know about your other account, which implies you’ve been **open about your boundaries** with him. This suggests you’re not naive about his character, but it also means you’re **willfully ignoring the harm he caused your sister**. - *Red flag*: If you’re using a throwaway account to avoid confronting G, that’s a sign you might be avoiding accountability for your own role in enabling the situation. --- ### **My Personal Take (Not Judgment, But Reflection)** I’d lean toward **this being a morally gray but ultimately flawed choice**, for these reasons: - **Friendship ≠ Loyalty to Betrayal**: A true friend doesn’t let someone they love suffer because of their actions. Even if you forgive G, your sister’s trust is a different currency. You can’t "reset" that by moving on. - **The Power Dynamic**: G has betrayed your sister, but you’re the one who’s been **shielding him** from consequences. That puts you in a position where you’re enabling his behavior, not just forgiving it. - **The Long-Term Cost**: Even if you’re not in the same state, **rumors and emotional baggage** follow people. If G’s behavior is a pattern, your sister’s pain might resurface later, and you’ll be the one she’s angry with for not standing up for her. That said, **I don’t think you’re an "asshole"**—you’re human, and you’re caught in a nightmare scenario where your best friend betrayed the person you love most. But I *do* think you’re **avoiding the harder conversation** about whether this friendship can survive the betrayal without resentment. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead** 1. **Set Boundaries with G** - You don’t have to cut him off, but you *can* make it clear that his actions with your sister are non-negotiable. Example: *"I forgive you, but I can’t ignore what you did to my sister. If this happens again, I’ll have to walk away."* 2. **Have an Honest Talk with Your Sister** - She might not expect you to "choose" sides, but she deserves to know you’re **aware of the harm** and that you’re not blindly defending G. You could say: *"I know this sucks, and I’m not happy about it either. But I also can’t just drop G—we’ve been friends too long. I’ll always have your back, but I’m not going to pretend this didn’t happen."* 3. **Reevaluate the Friendship** - Ask yourself: *Is this friendship worth the emotional toll on my sister?* If the answer is "yes," that’s fine—but be prepared for her to feel betrayed by you, not just G. 4. **Protect Your Own Peace** - If you’re truly okay with this, that’s your choice. But don’t pretend it’s not a **huge deal** for your sister. Acknowledge her pain, even if you’re not fixing it. --- ### **Final Answer: <0.5>** *(Not a full 1 because you’re not actively being malicious, but not a full 0 because you’re ignoring the harm to your sister.)* This is one of those situations where **no choice is perfect**, but **some choices are worse than others**. Your sister’s feelings matter just as much as your friendship with G—even if you can’t reconcile them. Would you like help brainstorming how to talk to either of them about this? You’re not alone in this mess.
